highlights.name: Orthonairovirus haemorrhagiae
highlights.headline: The most geographically widespread tick-borne virus causing human haemorrhagic fever; a WHO priority pathogen requiring high-level containment.

profile.headline: The most geographically widespread tick-borne virus causing human haemorrhagic fever; a WHO priority pathogen requiring high-level containment.
profile.syndrome: Abrupt fever, myalgia, severe headache, then haemorrhagic manifestations, hepatic dysfunction and DIC. Case fatality ranges from 5% to 40%. Nosocomial outbreaks among healthcare workers are a defining feature.
profile.transmission: Hyalomma tick bite, crushing infected ticks, contact with blood or tissues of viraemic livestock during slaughter, and person-to-person via blood and body fluids.
profile.reservoir: Ticks (transovarial and transstadial), with amplification in cattle, sheep, goats and hares — all of which remain healthy.
profile.geography: Africa, the Balkans, Middle East, Central and South Asia, western China; expanding with Hyalomma range into Spain and southern Europe.
profile.incubation: 1–9 days after tick bite; 5–13 days after blood contact.
profile.diagnosis: RT-PCR and antigen detection in BSL-4/BSL-3+ laboratories; IgM/IgG appear late and may be absent in fatal cases.
profile.management: Supportive with aggressive blood-product replacement; ribavirin is used widely though trial evidence is inconclusive.
profile.prevention: Tick protection, safe slaughter practice, and strict barrier nursing with full PPE. No licensed vaccine (a Bulgarian inactivated vaccine has limited use).
evidence: Extensive virologically confirmed outbreak and nosocomial transmission literature spanning sixty years.
